sect2.title: Creating animated brushes
sect2.para: Just like normal brushes, animated brushes can also be either grayscale or color. For grayscale images, where the actual brush will use the current foreground color, you use white for transparency. For color images, transparent parts are used as such and when making brush strokes, the actual colors will be used instead of the foreground color.

To create a new animated brush, create either a grayscale or color image, based on whether you want the brush to use the user's foreground color, or the actual colors in the image. Then create the images for your animation steps, called cells. You can choose to use one cell per layer, or divide each layer into multiple cells. To export the brush into gih format, select
File Export As… , name your work with the gih extension, and press the Export button. The following window is displayed:

sect3.title: Export Image as Brush Pipe

figure.title: Dialog to export an image as Brush Pipe

caption.para: Dialog to export an image as GIMP image hose

sect3.para: This dialog box has several options that allow you to select how your brush is animated.

listitem.para: The name of the brush that will be shown at the top of Brush Dialog in grid mode when the brush is selected.
Spacing is the distance between consecutive brush marks when you make a brush stroke with your pointing device. Consider drawing with a brush or other paint tool as a form of stamping.

With a low value for Spacing stamps will be very close and look continuous. With a high value the stamps will be separated which can give interesting results with a color brush (like the green pepper brush for instance).

This is a value in the range from 1 to 1000. This percentage refers to the brush diameter: 100% equals the diameter of the brush and would mean that the brush stamps appear next to each other but don't overlap.
The width and height of a cell describe the dimensions of a single brush image or stamp. By default a cell has the same size as your image. Each layer should have the same size.

A cell can never be larger than your image, but you can make a cell smaller. You could for example divide the image width and height by two and then have four cells per layer. Of course you then need to design four different brush images on each quarter of each layer that you intend to use.
When more than one cell fits on a layer, one or more guides appear that show where the layer will be divided.

For instance, say we want a 100×100 pixels brush with 8 different stamps. We can create these 8 stamps by making 8 layers of 100×100 pixels. Alternatively we can make one layer of 400×200 pixels and set the cell dimensions to 100×100; or a layer of 300×300 pixels with the same cell dimensions but then one cell will be unused.

The number of cells per layer. Each cell will be used as a separate brush stamp for the animation. Default (and maximum) is the amount of cells that fit in a layer based on the specified cell width and height.

This label appears only if you have more than one cell per layer or when an error was detected. It shows how the cells will be divided for each layer. If, for example, you have placed height cells at the rate of two cells per layer, GIMP will display: Displays as a 1 × 2 grid on each layer.
The number of dimensions determines how many factors (see Ranks below) will affect which brush stamp will be used. Up to 4 different ranks can be used.
Ranks are the factors that decide which brush stamp (cell) will be used when using an animated brush. The number entered here decides how many cells are available for this rank to choose from.

When exporting GIMP converts each cell to a separate brush image. When using the brush, GIMP stacks them into a FIFO stack (First In First Out: the first in is at the top of the stack and so can be first out). You can see this stack in the Layers Dialog of the resulting .gih image file.

In our example we use 4 layers with 2 cells each. From top to bottom: first cell of first layer, second cell of first layer, first cell of second layer, second cell of second layer, …, second cell of fourth layer. Whether you decide to use one cell per layer or several cells per layer, the end result is the same.
GIMP creates a computer array from this stack with the number of Dimensions you have set. You can use up to four dimensions, but in most cases one dimension is enough.

For two dimensions (2D), we talk about an array of rows (x axis) and columns (y axis).
When using three dimensions, often called 3D, we don't mention rows and columns, but use Dimensions and Ranks instead. The first dimension is along the x axis, the second dimension along the y axis, and the third along the z axis. Each dimension has ranks of cells.

To fill up this array, GIMP starts retrieving cells from the top of the stack. The way it selects cells is similar to that of an odometer: the rightmost rank digits change first. When they reach their maximum, the digits of the rank to the left start increasing.

For example, with an array(4,2,2), i.e. 4 choices for the first dimension, 2 choices for the second and third, you get the following succession: (1,1,1), (1,1,2), (1,2,1), (1,2,2), (2,1,1), (2,1,2), (2,2,2), (3,1,1), …, (4,2,2). We will see this later in an example.
For each rank, you can set how a cell is chosen from the amount of cells set in Ranks. The following Selection modes are the options that determine how the next brush image will be chosen:
GIMP selects the next cell within this rank for the current dimension, and at the last one goes back to the first.
GIMP selects a rank in the current dimension based on the current angle of the brush.
The first rank is for the direction 0°, upwards. The next ranks are selected clockwise depending on the angle and the amount chosen in ranks, which computes to 360 divided by the number of ranks.

So, with 4 ranks in the dimension, the angle will move 90° clockwise for each direction change: the second rank will be 90° (to the right), the third rank 180° (downwards) and the fourth rank will be at 270° (-90°).
GIMP selects a rank at random from the cells available for that dimension.
The cell to draw is selected based on one of the characteristics of your drawing device. Only works when your device supports this.
Most animated brushes use one dimension. This means there is only one characteristic that decides which brush cell will be used next.

A 1D brush can be visualized like this:
To create a brush like this, follow these steps:

step.para:
Select
File New… from the main menu.
Set Width and Height for example to 30 pixels.
In the Advanced Options, set the Color space to RGB color and set Fill with to Transparency.
Using the Text tool create 4 layers 1, 2, 3, 4. Delete the Background layer.

Select
File Save… from the main menu to first save your image as an .xcf file to keep its properties.

Select
File Export As… from the main menu to export the image as an animated brush with the .gih extension.

Browse to the location of the brushes directory located inside your personal GIMP configuration folder. This location can be found by going to the Brushes folder in Preferences and then click the file chooser button on the right.

In the Export Image as Brush Pipe dialog, provide a Description, set the Spacing (percent) to 100, set the Cell size to 30×30, set Dimension to 1, set Ranks to 4, and in the Selection drop-down select Incremental. Then click the Export button.

In the Brush Dialog, click the Refresh brushes
button.
Your brush appears among the other brushes, sorted alphabetically. You can use it immediately, without restarting GIMP.

Select your brush. Select a Paint tool, the Pencil tool for instance and use it to draw on a new image:
You see the digits 1, 2, 3, 4 appear in incremental order.

Reopen your .xcf brush image file and export it again as .gih. This time set the Selection drop-down to Random:
When using the brush the digits are now displayed in random order.
Now change the Selection drop-down to Angular and export again. The result is shown below:

listitem.para: We are now going to create a 3D animated brush: its orientation will vary according to the brush direction, it will alternate Left/Right hands regularly and its color will vary at random between black and blue.

The first question we have to answer to is the number of brush cells that we need to create. We will use the first dimension (x) for the brush direction (4 directions). The second dimension (y) is for choosing between Left and Right (2 cells()), and the third dimension (z) is for selecting the color (2 cells).

A 3D brush like that can be represented visually as follows:
There are 4 ranks in the first dimension (x), 2 ranks in the second dimension (y) and 2 ranks in the third dimension (z). Thus we need 4×2×2 = 16 image cells.

step.title: Create images for dimension 1 (x)
step.para:
Open a new 30×30 pixels image, RGB with Transparent Fill Type. Using the zoom draw a left hand with fingers upwards.
Ok, we are cheating here: our hand is borrowed from .
Save it as handL0k.xcf (hand Left 0° Black).
Open the Layers Dialog. Double click on the layer to open the Layer Attributes Dialog and rename it to handL0k.
Duplicate the layer. Leave only the duplicated layer visible. Select it and apply Layer TransformRotate 90° clockwise. Rename it to handL90k.xcf.
Repeat the same operations to create handL180k.xcf and handL-90k.xcf (or handL270k.xcf).

step.title: Create images for dimension 2 (y)
step.para: This dimension in our example has two ranks, one for the left hand and the other for the right hand. The left hand already exists. We create the right hand images by flipping the left hand horizontally.

Duplicate the handL0k layer. Make that the only visible layer and select it. Rename it to handR0K.xcf. Apply
Layer Transform Flip Horizontally .
Repeat the same operation on the other left hand layers to create their right hand equivalent.
Re-order layers to have a clockwise rotation from top to bottom, alternating Left and Right: handL0k, handR0k, handL90k, handR90k, …, handR-90k.

step.title: Create images for dimension 3 (z)
step.para: The third dimension has two ranks, one for black and the other blue hands. The first rank, black, already exists. All image cells of dimension three will be a copy, in blue, of the images of dimension two. This rquires a total of 16 images. However, a row of 16 layers can be cumbersome to manage. Therefor we will use layers with two image cells.

Select the handL0k layer and make it the only one visible. Use
Image Canvas Size…
to change the canvas size to 60×30 pixels.
Duplicate the handL0k layer. On the copy, fill the hand with blue using the Bucket Fill tool.

Now, select the Move tool. Check its Tool Options and set Tool Toggle (Shift) to Move the selected layers. Move the blue hand into the right part of the layer and align its edges with the corners of the image canvas. You can use Zoom or the arrow keys to make it easier to align it exactly where needed.

Make sure only handL0k and its blue copy are visible. Right click on the Layers dialog, then apply the Merge Visible Layers command with the option Expanded as necessary selected. The result is a 60×30 pixels layer with the black hand on the left and the blue hand on the right. Rename the layer to handsL0.
Repeat the same operations on the other layers.

step.title: Arrange layers in the correct order
step.para: The layers must be arranged in the correct order for GIMP to find the required image when using the brush. Our layers are already ordered the right way, but let's take a look at ordering to better understand how to do that manually.

There are two ways to think about this. The first method is mathematical: GIMP divides the 16 layers first by 4; that gives 4 groups of 4 layers for the first dimension. Each group represents a direction of the brush. Then, it divides each group by 2; that gives 8 groups of 2 layers for the second dimension: each group represents a left or right choice. Then another division by 2 for the third dimension to represent a color at random between black and blue.
The other method is visual, by using an array representation. The relationship between the two methods is shown in the image below:

para.emphasis: How will GIMP read this array?

step.para: GIMP starts with the first dimension which we set to Angular, for instance 90°. For the 90° rank, in yellow, in the second dimension, it selects a Left or Right hand, in an incremental way. Then, in the third dimension, it chooses from black or blue randomly. For this to work our layers must be in the following order:
No your animated brush is ready. Save it as .xcf first, then export as .gih with the following parameters:

listitem.para: Spacing: 100
Description: Hands
Cell Size: 30×30
Number of cells: 16
Dimensions: 3
Dimension 1: 4 ranks; Selection: Angular
Dimension 2: 2 ranks; Selection: Incremental
Dimension 3: 2 ranks; Selection: Random

step.para: Place your .gih file in GIMP's brush directory and refresh the brushes in the Brush dialog. You can now use your brush.
